extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of psychology, psychoanalysis, literary theory, and humour studies
extracted.subtask_description: Theoretical criteria and conditions Freud proposes for when something is comic, a joke, or humorous, including psychical mechanisms (difference in expenditure, discharge), situational factors, and genre-specific forms (mimicry, caricature, exposure).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rudimentary 'jokes' by modification/substitution are often mere nonsense
rubrics_metrics.description: Modifications and substitutions that only produce a familiar wording but add nothing fresh or serviceable should be regarded as nonsense rather than true jokes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such productions have 'freed themselves from one of the most essential characteristics of jokes' and may produce a comic effect only by their inadequacy; decide whether to call them 'bad' jokes or 'not jokes at all'. Example: facetious riddles whose answers rely on patently inadequate displacements (the 'herring' riddle).

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic can arise from uncovering unconscious thought-modes or by comparison with a complete joke
rubrics_metrics.description: Rudimentary joke-like nonsense may be comic either because it reveals unconscious modes of thought or because the pleasure arises from comparing it to a fully formed joke.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both sources can converge; the mere inadequacy of a support (i.e., failure to be a proper joke) can itself transform nonsense into comic nonsense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inadequacy relative to what ought to be effected produces irresistible comic
rubrics_metrics.description: When a riddle, joke, poem, or utterance fails to comply with essential conditions it can become irresistibly comic due to its absolute inadequacy rather than merely stupid or bad.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use examples of displaced explanations and failures of essential features (e.g., absurd answers defended by implausible displacements) to illustrate how inadequacy produces comic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic of speech is distinct from jokes; extreme clumsiness can be comic when sincerity disarms ridicule
rubrics_metrics.description: Poorly written or expressed verse and clumsy, limited thought can be comic not because they are jokes but because of the great distance between expectation and performance, especially if the author's good intentions and sincerity disarm mere annoyance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Kempner’s poems — their triteness and clumsiness yield comic effect when combined with the author's evident sincerity; without that sincerity similar products might only annoy rather than amuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Difference in expenditure is the basic determining condition of comic pleasure
rubrics_metrics.description: The origin of comic pleasure lies in a comparison of the difference between two expenditures (psychical cathexes); laughter arises when this difference is unutilizable and capable of discharge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the recognized surplus expenditure can be put to another use, comic pleasure fails. Just as jokes are constructed to prevent alternative use of the surplus, comic occurrences must isolate the surplus to permit discharge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surplus expenditure must be unutilizable and capable of discharge
rubrics_metrics.description: For comic pleasure to occur the difference in expenditure must not be utilisable elsewhere and must be capable of discharge; otherwise at best a fleeting sense of pleasure (not truly comic) results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This explains why many occasions with expenditure differences do not produce comic effect; special circumstances that prevent other uses of the surplus are required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cheerful mood ('inclined to laugh') is the most favourable condition
rubrics_metrics.description: A general cheerful disposition or euphoria predisposes one to find many things comic, by making smaller differences in expenditure sufficient to produce laughter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jokes and comic material often serve to restore this mood; in a cheerful state almost anything may be perceived as comic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expectation or attunement to the comic increases comic response
rubrics_metrics.description: Being prepared to experience the comic (e.g., going to a farce or reading a comic book) lowers the threshold for recognizing small differences as comic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Communicated intention to be amused can produce laughter even before any comedic stimulus acts; people may later feel ashamed at what they laughed at because of this anticipatory effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ongoing imaginative or intellectual work inhibits comic pleasure
rubrics_metrics.description: Serious intellectual or imaginative activity occupies cathexes needed for discharge and thus interferes with the generation of comic pleasure; only unusually large differences break through such engagement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Abstract reflection leaves no place for the comic except when interrupted; thus professionals (examiners, instructors) often fail to see the comic in situations where lay observers laugh.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focused attention on the comparison prevents the comic — it must be automatic/preconscious
rubrics_metrics.description: If attention is concentrated on the comparison that could produce the comic, the effect is lost; the comic process must proceed automatically in the preconscious without the cathexis of conscious attention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This explains why experts (with standards clearly before them) are annoyed rather than amused by errors that others find laughable; the comic cannot bear hypercathexis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Release of strong affect blocks comic discharge
rubrics_metrics.description: Situations that generate intense affect (pity, anger, distress) typically prevent the discharge of surplus expenditure necessary for comic pleasure, except in special cases where a large difference forces an automatism of release.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: laughter in the midst of strong emotion can occur when the magnitude of the disappointment itself forces a laugh (Colonel Butler example). Generally, the comic emerges most readily in more or less indifferent cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleasurable accompanying circumstances can encourage comic pleasure (contagion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Other pleasurable factors present in a situation can boost the emergence of comic pleasure, analogous to a contagious or fore-pleasure effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These ancillary pleasures make it easier for surplus cathexis to discharge as laughter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic of sexuality/obscenity often derives from exposure and perceived omission of expenditure
rubrics_metrics.description: Exposure becomes comic because observers compare the ease of obtaining the sight with the great expenditure that would otherwise have been required to conceal it; the exposed person becomes the comic object.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Witnessing an exposure is not necessarily comic for the direct witness (who experiences sexual pleasure), but recounting it or making it second-hand restores the comic by reinstating the sense of omitted concealment; sexuality offers many occasions for comic pleasure alongside erotic excitement (degradation, unmasking).

rubrics_metrics.name: Infantile (childish) elements underpin many forms of the comic
rubrics_metrics.description: Many comic effects trace back to infantile features — excess movement, limited intellectual expenditure, pleasure in repetition, mimicry, lack of proportion — so the comic often involves rediscovering the child in another or oneself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bergson’s ideas ('mechanization of life') are related but Freud emphasizes that the comic depends on comparison that touches childish nature, not necessarily recollected childhood pleasures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Children lack the fully developed 'comic feeling'; adult comic arises as regained 'lost laughter of childhood'
rubrics_metrics.description: Children laugh for direct, comprehensible motives (superiority, pleasure) but lack the preconscious comparative standard adults use; adults' comic feeling often substitutes for motives children retain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The comic requires a standard of comparison ('this is how I did it' vs 'this is how he does it') that children do not possess until socialization provides it; thus child laughter differs qualitatively from adult comic laughter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three loci of comic comparison: other vs self / within other / within self
rubrics_metrics.description: The comic difference can arise from (a) comparing another person to oneself (comic of movement, form, character), (b) a comparison wholly within the other person (situation, exaggeration, mimicry, degradation, unmasking), or (c) a comparison within oneself (comic of expectation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Map forms to loci: (a) yields comic from resemblance to childishness; (b) includes situations based on embarrassment, repetition, exaggeration tied to the child's lack of proportion, and mimicry as a child's art; (c) (expectation) is the remotest in children and develops late.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mimicry, exaggeration (caricature), degradation and unmasking have infantile bases and produce comic pleasure
rubrics_metrics.description: Mimicry (a child's primary game), exaggeration (childish lack of proportion), degradation (adult condescension to children), and unmasking (derived from degradation) are major mechanisms of the comic tied to childhood dynamics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use examples of mimicry and adults lowering themselves to children's level to illustrate how these mechanisms transform pleasure in children into comic pleasure for adults.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repetition frequently produces comic effect; moderation and restraint are late cultural acquisitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Repetition appeals to the child’s pleasure in constant repetition and thus yields comic pleasure in adults when exploited (e.g., repeated misfortunes becoming comic).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Mark Twain’s story of the cow falling through the roof repeatedly; the forty-sixth night comment makes the repetition comic. Repetition is one mechanism among many that isolate surplus cathexis for discharge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humour operates as an economy of affect and differs from public comic pleasure
rubrics_metrics.description: Humour permits pleasurable response despite circumstances that would ordinarily release distressing affect; it substitutes for release by suppressing affect in statu nascendi and can be contained within a single person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Humour completes its course within an individual and need not be communicated; examples include Galgenhumor (gallows humour) and Mark Twain’s anecdotal economy of pity, where humorous framing prevents full pity and converts it into pleasure.
